record.title: Oral History Interview with Mike Morrow (part 1)

point.title: Introduction
point.partial_transcript: This is Joanna Jou. Today is October 28th, 2025.
point.synopsis: Joanna Jou begins the interview and introduces the narrator, Mike Morrow.

point.title: Family History and Childhood
point.partial_transcript: And I wanted to start off with if you can tell me where and when you were born.
point.synopsis: Mike Morrow details how his parents met, when and where he was born, and his childhood growing up in the countryside. His childhood was disrupted by his mother's nervous breakdown.
point.keywords: Seattle; Washington; Canada; Canadian; Renton; Countryside; Father; Mother; Washington State; WA; Greenwood; Wenatchee

point.title: Time at the Seattle World's Fair and First Exposure to Dartmouth
point.partial_transcript: And then I went off to Dartmouth, and that was kind of a fluke that I went to Dartmouth.
point.synopsis: Morrow recounts his time as a Pedicab driver during the Seattle World's Fair, when he met two Dartmouth students who inspired him to go to school there.
point.keywords: Seattle World's Fair; Seattle; Dartmouth; Pedicab; Cycle Rickshaw; Century 21 Exposition; Dartmouth College
point.subjects: Century 21 Exposition; Seattle; Dartmouth College; Cycle Rickshaw

point.title: Arrival at Dartmouth and Student Life
point.partial_transcript: I mean, I actually drove across country. I got a ride with a guy I found online—not online.
point.synopsis: Morrow talks about his cross country journey to get to Dartmouth, and what Dartmouth was like once he arrived. Morrow took his studies seriously and did not see himself as social, which stood in contrast to the overwhelming, party-based culture that Morrow experienced on campus. Morrow, at Jou's request, clarifies his parents' names and backgrounds as well as when he matriculated at Dartmouth.

point.title: Switch from English Major to Spanish and Latin American Literature
point.partial_transcript: Great. And I know we were just talking about your time at Dartmouth so sorry that I cut you off,
point.synopsis: Morrow begins his discussion about how his academic interests changed while at Dartmouth. Unsatisfied with his English major, Morrow switched to studying Spanish and Latin American literature, which he liked much more. He attributes the switch, in part, to his father, who had given him a non-conformist world view and an interest in the contemporary world.
point.keywords: English; Spanish; Literature; English Literature; Spanish Literature; Academic Major; Dartmouth; Dartmouth College; Latin American Literature; English-language literature; English major

point.title: Passion for Spanish Literature from Childhood Ethical Tension
point.partial_transcript: And so I grew up with this tension between my mother's very Orthodox Catholicism and my father's total contempt for all religious orthodoxy.
point.synopsis: Morrow discusses how his mother's highly religious worldview clashed with that of his father. While Morrow's mother was a devout Catholic, his father rejected religion and was agnostic. These two contrasting viewpoints made life very difficult for him as he attempted to rationalize the two opposing viewpoints. Morrow believes this contrast in ethical, religious, and moral worldviews contributed to his mother's nervous breakdown, though he also acknowledges that his own nervous breakdown may have also caused it. This tension served as the origin for his passion for Spanish and Latin American literature at Dartmouth, which also explored the tension within Catholicism.
point.keywords: Catholicism; Orthodoxy; Conflict; Nervous breakdown; Relgion; Morality; Ethics; Mental breakdown; Dartmouth College; Dartmouth; Spanish Literature; Latin American Literature
point.subjects: Catholicism; orthodoxy; conflict; mental breakdown; religion; morality; ethics; internal conflict; Spanish literature; Latin American literature; Dartmouth College

point.title: Switch to International Relations Major
point.partial_transcript: I discovered that Dartmouth had a major called International Relations, which I never even heard of actually before, so I actually transferred again.
point.synopsis: Inspired by his time studying Spanish and Latin American Literature, Morrow and a trip to Europe he took with his brother during the summer following his freshman year, Morrow changed his major to International Relations. He liked International Relations as it gave him the opportunity to study many different disciplines and allowed him to engage with cultures that weren't his own. He still views International Relations as a good major and still recommends it to his younger friends today.
point.keywords: International Relations; Academic Major; Dartmouth; Dartmouth College
point.subjects: Dartmouth College; academic major; international relations

point.title: The Summer of Sophomore Year and Introduction to Chinese at Dartmouth
point.partial_transcript: In the summer of my—between my sophomore and junior year, I guess, second and third year, I got a job working as a choker setter up in the woods
point.synopsis: Morrow, who initially planned to study Japanese at the University of Washington, Seattle, ended up signing up for Chinese at Dartmouth and getting a job in the logging industry as a choker setter over the summer. Morrow wanted to study Japanese because he had gotten interested in Buddhism and a mentor of his, Ernest P. Young, was teaching, but a bulletin posting about a Chinese class at Dartmouth with limited spots convinced him to go back to Hanover to study in the fall. Morrow was briefly interrupted at the beginning of this segment.
point.keywords: Choker setter; Japanese; Seattle; Washington; Chinese
point.subjects: Choker setter; Japanese; Seattle; Washington; Chinese

point.title: Chinese class at Dartmouth / Decision to go to Taiwan
point.partial_transcript: Knowing this, I knew nothing about what I was getting into, but Dartmouth had hired Henry [C.] Fenn, who had just retired from Yale, to start their Chinese program.
point.synopsis: Morrow recounts the academically challenging Chinese class he took at Dartmouth. The class was taught by Henry C. Fenn, a professor known for his work developing the "Yale Method" (also known as Yale romanization of Mandarin) during World War Two to help American soldiers learn the language. The course was challenging and many other students dropped out, but he persevered. This course, along with other developments in East and Southeast Asia, inspired him to drop Spanish Literature and go fully into Chinese Language. He believes that decision was a pivotal moment in his life. Additionally, Ernie Young, a Professor who Morrow had developed a strong relationship with during his time at Dartmouth, offered Morrow the opportunity to go with him to Taiwan. Morrow, who had completed his degree requirements, decided to go.
point.keywords: Chinese; Mandarin; Chinese Language; Mandarin Language; Dartmouth College; China; Taiwan
point.subjects: Chinese; Yale romanization of Mandarin; Standard Chinese; Yale romanization of Mandarin; Dartmouth College; China; Mandarin; Taiwan

point.title: Life in Taiwan and Move to Vietnam
point.partial_transcript: I ended up going there and they went back. I stayed.
point.synopsis: Morrow went to Taiwan with Professor Young, and he decided to stay in the country after Young left. During his time in Taiwan, he met many U.S. soldiers, who were on leave from the Vietnam War at the Taiwanese R&R center. While Morrow was skeptical of U.S. foreign policy at this time, he had not been a part of the opposition to the war at Dartmouth. As an International Relations student, Morrow was captivated by Vietnam and decided to ditch his plans to return home and fly to Vietnam, where he declared himself a journalist. He ended up living in Cholon, Saigon, and he never went back to Dartmouth. Morrow also clarifies at the end of the segment that he was working on an oral history project while in Taiwan and that Young had left Taiwan after one semester.
point.keywords: Taiwan; R&R; Vietnam; Vietnam War; Dartmouth; Dartmouth College; Ernest P. Young; Ernie Young
point.subjects: Taiwan; Vietnam; Vietnam War; R&R; Dartmouth College; Ernest P. Young

point.title: Journey to Taiwan and Experience of Authoritarian Rule Under Chiang Kai-shek
point.partial_transcript: And were there any significant events or moments that you remember during this period in terms of the political atmosphere?
point.synopsis: Morrow describes his journey from Seattle to Taiwan, which passed through Tokyo, Japan. Morrow recalls an anecdote about watching two Japanese airport staff playing catch with a baseball at the Tokyo Airport. Morrow recalls his experience living under the authoritarian rule of Chiang Kai-shek in Taiwan, which was in the midst of a campaign to repress communism. Morrow got in trouble for speaking out against the regime and for interviewing dissident Peng Ming-min, which led to an encounter with the police. He did not pay much attention to what was going on back in the United States, even once he had moved to Vietnam. It was only later in life, as a result of the internet, that he begun to re-engage with American society.
point.keywords: Japan; Tokyo; Taiwan; Chiang Kai-shek; Authoritarianism; Taipei; Jiang Jieshi

point.title: Family reaction to Morrow's time in Asia and his Mother's recovery.
point.partial_transcript: And how did your parents feel after they learned about you staying in Asia?
point.synopsis: Morrow details his family's reactions to his travels in Asia, and his unexpected decision to go to Vietnam. His father was supportive and understood his decision, sending him money when he ran out and visiting him once in Saigon. As Morrow became more critical of the war, his father, who was a working class Democrat, also became more outspoken in his opposition to support his son. Morrow's trip to Asia also seemed to help his mother recover, who became very worried for him. However, Morrow also posits that his father's death played a larger role in his mother regaining her sanity.

point.title: Reflection on his Father's Influence
point.partial_transcript: Great. Awesome. I think this is a good time to end our first session.
point.synopsis: Morrow reflects further on his relationship with his father. While his mother was sick, Morrow's relationship with his father was very important to him, and greatly influenced him. His father's time as a migrant worker inspired Morrow to become a migrant worker over the summer when he was 16. His father encouraged him to do many high-risk and dangerous activities, which Morrow himself would not allow his children to do now. His father was very supportive to him, and only after his father died did he really appreciate that fully. Morrow realized that although he was more educated than his father, his father was a wise man.
point.keywords: Father; Son; Migrant Worker; Encouragement; Relationship

WEBVTT
NOTE TRANSCRIPTION BEGIN
00:00:01.312 --> 00:00:22.922 <v JOU> This is Joanna Jou. Today is October 28th, 2025. I am conducting this oral history interview for the Dartmouth Vietnam Project. I am conducting this interview with Mr. Michael [David] Morrow, and it is taking place virtually on Zoom today. Mr. Morrow, thank you for speaking to me today.
00:00:22.922 --> 00:00:24.569 <v MORROW> You're welcome, Joanna.
00:00:24.569 --> 00:00:33.000 <v JOU> And I wanted to start off with if you can tell me where and when you were born.
00:00:33.000 --> 00:01:31.322 <v MORROW> I was born July 24th, 1945 in Seattle, Washington. My parents had met during the Aleutian Campaign in Prince Rupert, British Columbia. My mother is Canadian. My father is American. Prince Rupert was the base for the joint American-Canadian task force that had the mission to liberate the Aleutian Islands after the Japanese had occupied it. I'm a product of that period. My mother, who was pregnant with me, moved to Seattle just a short time before I was born.
00:01:31.322 --> 00:01:47.602 <v JOU> And did you grow up in—were you born and raised in Seattle? And also, if you can tell me a little bit more about your family and your childhood, such as siblings and upbringing.
00:01:47.602 --> 00:03:42.000 <v MORROW> I was born in Seattle and my family lived in Seattle, very close to where my paternal grandfather and his family had homesteaded in Seattle way back in the 19th century, in what is now called the Greenwood area of North Seattle. But when I was about five going on six years old, my parents moved into the countryside, east of Seattle, into the foothill areas of the mountain—on the edge of the mountains. It was my father's goal that we—his intention that we—my brother—I have only one brother who is twenty-one months, a little less than two years, younger than myself. It was my father's intention, particularly that we not grow up in the city, but that we grow up in the countryside. And he and my mother bought a ten acre, what you would call a stump ranch. It wasn't really a commercial farm, but it was a place on the edge of the forest where we kept a few animals. And my father and mother both worked. My father was an electrician. My mother was a nurse in the hospital of Renton, which is a suburb of Seattle now. But at that time, we were still quite far out into the countryside.
00:03:42.000 --> 00:05:50.000 <v MORROW> And my brother and I went to school in Renton, which was about a three and a half mile commute into the city. My father would generally drive us in on his way to work and we would find our way home; sometimes hitchhiking home, sometimes waiting for my father. We grew up like that until I was in the second year of high school. And my mother, who had worked very hard as a nurse in the Renton General Hospital, mostly working nights in the emergency ward, sometimes in maternity. My mother had a nervous breakdown, quite a serious nervous breakdown, and this was very disruptive for our family. My mother, being a Canadian, she was able to get mental health treatment in Canada. The family was somewhat divided. My mother was institutionalized for a while, had shock treatment. It was a difficult period. My father, my brother, and I moved much farther east. We moved over the mountains into eastern Washington, into quite a rural community called East Wenatchee; it's in the Wenatchee Valley. We finished growing up there, my mother eventually. I used to commute in the summer time, or when we had vacation time, I would go up to Canada to visit my mother when she was still in hospital, in mental hospital.
00:05:50.000 --> 00:06:46.000 <v MORROW> Eventually, she came back to the family, but was never really functional again as a mother, at least while I was still growing up. And so my father and my brother and I, we made a life for ourselves. We still—we had, again, a small piece of land. I lived close to the countryside. I had a horse, hunted in the countryside with my classmates, some of whom had ranches. I would go out into the—I spent a lot of time in the countryside when I was a boy.
00:06:46.000 --> 00:09:55.000 <v MORROW> And then I went off to Dartmouth, and that was a fluke that I went to Dartmouth. The Seattle World's Fair had happened in Seattle just as I was completing my third year of high school in the Wenatchee Valley. As soon as school was out, I went over to Seattle to go to the fair. I was very eager to have an opportunity to participate in what was an international event. And I met two young fellows who had just come out from Dartmouth, who had gotten jobs driving pedicabs. The Taiwanese style pedicab that had been brought from Taiwan and had been deployed in the fairground as a taxi device. I thought that was really interesting. I was reasonably athletic and it seemed like a really interesting job. I met these guys—while they were sitting on their cabs, talked with them, asked how you got a job like that, went and applied, got a job as a pedicab driver. And I got to know these guys well enough. They were older than me; I think they were in their second, third year of university. And I became a pedicab driver at the Seattle World's Fair. I think I was the youngest pedicab driver there. And I spent the summer driving pedicab, and I learned a little bit about Dartmouth, which was attractive to me because they had skiing. I was a good student. I became the salutatorian of my graduating class. But anyway, I applied to Dartmouth just because I liked these guys and they told me it was a good place to ski. I didn't know anything about it really. And I got into Dartmouth. And then I went off to Dartmouth. And that was the completion of my youth.
00:09:55.000 --> 00:14:16.365 <v MORROW> I actually drove across country. I got a ride with a guy I found online—not online. I found through some kind of—there was no online; I found through some kind of an advertisement, I can't remember, who was going to Yale and he was also an upperclassman and I shared the driving responsibilities with him. He had a little Volkswagen. We drove across the country and I arrived at Hanover knowing very little and quite a fish out of water because at that time, at least, Dartmouth was a very preppy place, and I was anything but—I was a country kid. And I was quite ill prepared in the sense that I had gone to a very small high school and I had very little access to the intellectual stimulation that a lot of my classmates had, but I was extremely eager. And I fell in love with the Dartmouth library. It was amazing to me that there was all these books. And I became a student at Dartmouth in a different way from most of my classmates in that I was extremely serious. Dartmouth then was somewhat in the image of, you know, Animal House. It was a place where you drank too much. People, although they were intellectually qualified, it was not really popular to try very hard, or to at least let other people know that you were trying very hard. And it was this rogue place in the Ivy League where you wore heavy boots and jeans, and some a red and black mackinaw. It had this backwards style to it. Of course, there were no women in the student body then. And so it was a little bit rougher, but I didn't—to me, this was an overwhelming experience. And my family was also not wealthy and so I took my responsibilities to study; not just to study, to learn very, very seriously, maybe too seriously. So I basically lived in the library and just read all the time. And I was as interested in reading as I was in reading what was required in my courses. I really did very little other than go to class and go to the library. I wasn't a social student. I wasn't interested in much of what Dartmouth was supposed to be about, including going to football games and making bonfires and all of this stuff. It all seemed rather silly to me.
00:14:16.365 --> 00:14:25.094 <v JOU> Just for the record, what were your parents' and brother's name?
00:14:25.094 --> 00:14:27.000 <v MORROW> What were my parents' names?
00:14:27.000 --> 00:14:29.449 <v JOU> Yes.
00:14:29.449 --> 00:16:25.273 <v MORROW> Sorry, I didn't—my father's name was John Morrow, John David Morrow. I have his second name also: Michael David Morrow. My mother is from Polish immigrant stock, originally from Saskatchewan, in the middle of Canada. My grandparents were essentially Polish peasants who got free land in Canada. My father's background is mixed Irish and Irish American. Part of the family came with the potato famine, part of them were old immigrants from the Appalachia, who had come out. Only my grandmother, in fact, was born on the second wagon train coming out from St. Louis [MO] to Seattle and the Snake River Valley in Idaho, almost died. Her mother died giving birth to her, and she was actually saved by the daughter of Chief Seattle, or Chief Sealth, who was the native chief in the Seattle area at that time. She nursed my mother and my grandmother. So I have that tradition on my father's side. Anyway, my father's name was John David Morrow and my mother's name was Josephine Olive Rubleski, which is a fairly common Polish name.
00:16:25.273 --> 00:16:29.037 <v JOU> And your brother's name?
00:16:29.037 --> 00:16:37.283 <v MORROW> My brother's name is Peter Morrow, Peter John Morrow. So he has my father's first name as his second name.
00:16:37.283 --> 00:16:46.000 <v JOU> Alright, awesome. Thank you. And what year did you matriculate into Dartmouth?
00:16:46.000 --> 00:16:58.471 <v MORROW> I guess it was—I'm the class of '67. So I guess I went, it was the September of '63.
00:16:58.471 --> 00:17:24.420 <v JOU> Great. And I know we were just talking about your time at Dartmouth so sorry that I cut you off, but going a little more into depth with your time here, I was wondering if you can talk about what you studied here and your student life.
00:17:24.420 --> 00:22:18.000 <v MORROW> I started out as an English major. I was always interested—from the time I was in high school, I'd been interested in writing and had written a bit. I didn't do very well as an English major. I started in the first year, and then I realized that—I don't know what—I realized. First of all, I had no real literary background. I was way behind my contemporaries, but there were one or two professors who were sympathetic or empathetic to my interest. I also found being an English major somewhat esoteric. I myself was already very interested in the contemporary world. I had grown up in a way that I was quite proactive or engaged in, I don't know, on the margins of society. I was always something of a nonconformist or somebody a little bit alienated, or on the edge of my own society. Some of this perhaps encouraged by my father, who was that way. I was also somewhat political, again, maybe encouraged by my father. So anyway, I dropped—I changed, initially to study Spanish literature, which I'd studied some Spanish and I'd taken two years of Spanish in high school. I didn't have very much Spanish, but I had enough to get a threshold. I liked that a great deal more because at least at the level we were studying Spanish literature at Dartmouth, we were being introduced to a new culture basically, in a very elementary way. Into Spanish literature in a way that was not true with English language and English literature, in which you had this whole body of literature that was somewhat overwhelming to me. I mean, going all the way back to Beowulf and Shakespeare, and then all of the contemporary and American and British and English literature and so on. Anyway, and also I think another thing that was interesting to me about Spanish literature and about Latin American literature was this tension with Catholic culture. Because in my own upbringing, my mother was to the day she died, a very conservative Catholic. I mean, she died with rosary beads in her hands as a very old woman. But my father was from this Irish background. And my father always said there are three kinds of Irish. There are the Catholics, there are the Protestants, and then there are the Irish who hate all priests. I was told by my father from the time I was very young that we were of that third type.
00:22:18.000 --> 00:24:17.000 <v MORROW> And so I grew up with this tension between my mother's very Orthodox Catholicism and my father's total contempt for all religious orthodoxy. And there was a irony in that because, at least in my mind, my father was in some ways, always—in my view anyway—the more ethical of my two parents. And if I look back, I have to say that my mother's nervous breakdown, I think, was caused in part by the tensions that existed in our family and her worries about how my brother and I were going to turn out under the influence of my agnostic—if not atheistic—father. And I neglected to say that when I was twelve, thirteen, I had a nervous breakdown. Actually, maybe it was my nervous breakdown, just as I was becoming an adolescent, probably triggered my mother's nervous breakdown, which was far more serious in her case. I had gone through this very difficult period as an adolescent, which was actually, again with reflection, a result of trying to rationalize the contradictory ethical systems or moralities of my mother and my father. They were irreconcilable actually. There's a whole story about how I got through that and out of it, but I won't go into it now.
00:24:17.000 --> 00:28:25.000 <v MORROW> But anyway, I had arrived at Dartmouth with all of this baggage and Spanish literature—and especially the period we ended up studying, which was the late nineteenth century and early into the mid twentieth century—was very preoccupied with this crisis—existential crisis—of Catholicism. And I ended up really in love with philosopher writers like Unamuno—Miguel de Unamuno—, Pio Barroja, [Jorge Luis] Borges, and on the Latin American side, people like Borges and so on. And so I developed this passion for Spanish literature and Latin American literature. And out of that came a real interest. I discovered that Dartmouth had a major called International Relations, which I never even heard of actually before, so I actually transferred again. I moved my major into International Relations and I thought I was going to be a Latin American scholar. And I was particularly interested in Chile and the Dominican Republic and somewhat in Mexico and all of these places. And then in the summer after my freshman year, my brother and I went—my brother was still in high school, but we got a cheap flight to Europe and we hitchhiked around Europe and including going to Spain for a short time. That experience with Europe, a very brief and somewhat naive experience—a very naive experience—really triggered my interest in international relations and breaking out of my own culture and having experiences that would take me somewhere else. I think, in part, it was almost escapist because I was still running away, I think, from my own youth, which had been somewhat, I don't know, it was just somewhat complicated and troubled. Anyway, we'd gone to Europe, come back. I'd gotten interested in Spanish literature and Latin American literature and then international relations. And that gave me the opportunity to engage politics and economics and history. And it's a great major for somebody like me. I still recommend it to young friends. At least the way it was taught at Dartmouth, you made up your own major. You could take courses right across the board, even in things like anthropology or literature, or whatever; you could take a wide range of subjects and they would be accepted.
00:28:25.000 --> 00:33:30.000 <v MORROW> In the summer of my [Morrow interrupted]. In the summer of my—between my sophomore and junior year, I guess, second and third year, I got a job working as a choker setter up in the woods, working for a warehouser up on Mount St. Helens, the mountain that blew up Southern Washington. A choker setter is the lowest of the low in the timber trade. You go out and you can belt these logs in the bush and they pull them up, get them to a landing up on some logging road and they're loaded onto trucks take out. It's a dirty, difficult job and you work with real tough people. Anyway, I got off to do this and I also went off with a couple other guys from Dartmouth and we spent the summer doing that. And then the next summer I decided I wanted to study Japanese language because I'd become interested in Buddhism, and I'd taken one course in oriental philosophy at Dartmouth. I was more interested in Buddhism, maybe because it was somewhat trendy then. A guy named Alan [Wilson] Watts, who was a popularizer of Zen, but it wasn't offered at Dartmouth. I was going to take a summer course at the University of Washington studying Japanese. And it was also somewhat influenced because there was a young teacher at Dartmouth who had become a mentor of mine. Ernie [Ernest P.] Young went on to become head of the—I guess—Chinese studies or Asian studies. I think Chinese history department is what it was at Michigan State, but he was an undergraduate student teaching. And he had been an aide to Ambassador [Edwin O.] Reischauer in Japan, but he was also a student of China and he was attached to the Yenching Institute at Harvard and he was doing a PhD on China. Anyway, I had decided I was going to study Japanese, and it was—actually, I just realized I made a mistake. It wasn't the summer of my junior year. That was too late because the summer that I ended up going off and working for a warehouse in southern Washington in the timber. I did that—initially, I wasn't going to work. I was going to try and get a part-time job in Seattle and study Japanese that year. Anyway, when I went in to register for my courses, for September, I discovered that there was a bulletin on the board there saying that Chinese would be offered the next semester, and there were limited spaces to sign up. And so on the spot, and the way you do these things when you're young, I decided well I wouldn't study Japanese in Seattle. I would sign up and get one of these spaces to study Chinese the next fall at Dartmouth. And that would leave me free to try and find a better paying job. And then that's how I ended up going and spending the summer in the woods on Mount St. Helen as a choker setter. I eventually became what's called a third rigger, which is a promotion. But anyway, I had a hard summer, but a good summer working and came back to Dartmouth.
00:33:30.000 --> 00:36:53.000 <v MORROW> Knowing this, I knew nothing about what I was getting into, but Dartmouth had hired Henry [C.] Fenn, who had just retired from Yale, to start their Chinese program. Henry [C.] Fenn was famous in Chinese language studies. He developed what was called the "Yale Method" during World War Two for training intelligence officers very quickly in Chinese. And he brought all of that to Dartmouth so we ended up—those of us who signed up for that course, and initially quite a few people signed up. I think there were over twenty, but it was the only course that met at eight o'clock in the morning six days a week; and with smart quizzes twice a week, you couldn't miss a class because if you weren't there for a smart quiz, then half your grade was based on how you did on the smart quizzes. And so after a very short period of time, a lot of people dropped out. And I don't know, by the time we finished that first semester, I think there were only five or six of us left. It was also graded on a bell curve and there was one Swiss exchange student who already spoke three or four languages—wanted to be an interpreter—and he was so much better than all the rest of us. He set the curve very, very high. And it was a sadistic experience to stay in that class, but I was determined to stay in, but in the course of staying in and learning some—I did learn some Chinese. I was trying to stick—I was still convinced that I was going to be a Latin American scholar and this Chinese thing was a lark. It broadened my cultural knowledge. But of course, the Vietnam War was happening, and the Cultural Revolution was happening, and China was becoming more and more interesting. And Chinese language was so hard; I eventually dropped Spanish, threw myself into the Chinese, and that really changed my life because, as I often say, I wish I could come back and live a second life and I would live it in Spanish, but I—the life I ended up living has been greatly influenced by that decision to take, join, and stick with that very difficult Chinese course at Dartmouth.
00:36:53.000 --> 00:39:41.000 <v MORROW> Anyway I went on and then didn't—I've become closer and closer to Ernie Young who considered me a very good student of Chinese history. I took courses with him on Asia, basically on Chinese history. And he had given me—I was a good student at Dartmouth. I often got straight A's. I often got—I did well, and I especially did well in these courses that interested me. And I got—I don't know if Dartmouth still has this, but if you did especially well in a course, you got a commendation. I earned at least one of those, I think, in Chinese history and got close to Ernie Young and he was—he wanted to recommend me to go on to the Yenching Institute and study Chinese history and so on. I thought that sounded good and that was going to be my future somehow. He was a hero for me. Anyway, the next summer he said, "I'm going to Taiwan to—I have to complete my PhD." He was doing his PhD on Yuan Shikai, the founding president of the Chinese Republic after the collapse of the Qing Dynasty. And his wife was also a China scholar, Marilyn Young. And they had a couple of kids. And he was saying, "you can come with us. I'll take responsibility for you. You take a semester off from Dartmouth." And by this time, I always took extra courses at Dartmouth. Also, I was one of these people who was very insecure at Dartmouth and I thought I'd never get an opportunity like this again to learn. And so I—at that time, I don't know what your curriculum's like now, but we had normally only three courses a quarter, but I would take four. To me, it was joy because I was just soaking up so much knowledge.
00:39:41.000 --> 00:45:30.777 <v MORROW> Anyway, this opportunity to go to Taiwan with Ernie and Marilyn and study Chinese in Taiwan. And also, I could do a history project while I was there, something that he would be my mentor for. And I had already completed because I'd already completed my international relations degree—the requirements for my international relations degree, so I wasn't particularly under any pressure to come back and take required courses. I ended up going there and they went back. I stayed. I decided I would take my senior year. I would just delay my graduation and stay there. I'd gotten part-time work teaching English and I could finance myself. And at that time, Taiwan was very cheap. And I lived very simply. I rented a room from a Chinese family and just lived a student's life in Taiwan. And then, of course, the Vietnam War had come along, and it was, I mean, there were even, Taiwan was then an R&R [rest and recuperation] center for soldiers coming who were—during the Vietnam War, the typical soldier who was deployed to Vietnam was only deployed for a year, which was silly because they never learned anything about Vietnam. By the time they learned something, they were being sent home, let's put it that way. But during that year, they were also given a week's break or so to go to what were called R&R centers. They were all over. They were in Singapore; Bangkok; you could go back to Hawaii; you could go to Tokyo; you could go to Manila; you could go to Taipei. So I started running into some of these soldiers. And of course, I had also—in the course of doing my degree—I'd taken a course in Southeast Asian history also. And I knew a little bit about Vietnam, not very much, but because I was interested in international relations and Vietnam was becoming—by 1966/67, it was a real topic, including on the Dartmouth campus. I was not, although many people think I probably was because I became quite outspoken about the war later, but when I was at Dartmouth, there was a left-wing radical opposition to the war. I wasn't part of it. In fact, I had been very much influenced by Hans Morgenthau's realism. I had a skepticism about American foreign policy, but I was not decided even about whether the US should be in Vietnam, should not be in Vietnam. But anyway, I was forced by the circumstance or chose under the influence of the circumstance to consider Vietnam more and more centrally in my own formation as somebody who by this time was thinking he was going to be a professional and somehow involved with international relations and American foreign policy and so on. So eventually I, without telling my parents or anybody else, I traded in my return ticket to go back home for a one way ticket to Vietnam, and I bought a camera and a manual typewriter and made my way to Vietnam on a tourist visa and declared myself a journalist without any real bona fides. And I had I think 67 dollars or something in my pocket when I arrived and a note from a Taiwanese student friend to his parents who lived down in Cholon—the Chinatown of Saigon—and I ended up there. And as things turned out, and it's a long story, but I never went back to Dartmouth, and Dartmouth disowned me afterwards so now I'm here.
00:45:30.777 --> 00:45:44.856 <v JOU> So you leave to Taiwan, and then Ernie Young and his wife came back to U.S., and then you stayed in Taiwan.
00:45:44.856 --> 00:47:02.760 <v MORROW> They had stayed only for one semester—yeah, two quarters, I guess. Ernie was doing some archive research for his own PhD, and then he had to go back to teach. And initially, I was only supposed to be there for that period also. I guess it was only one quarter. It was a summer plus one quarter. And they went back, but I said, "I'm just going to stay on. I'll spend the rest of the academic year here" because I was learning a lot of Chinese. I started an oral history project and I was deep into that and I thought, "I'm learning more here than I'll learn back at Dartmouth." Anyway, one thing led to the other and I ended up going to Vietnam, but not back to Dartmouth. They went back and that was the last I ever saw of them and the last I ever saw of Dartmouth.
00:47:02.760 --> 00:47:13.114 <v JOU> And were there any significant events or moments that you remember during this period in terms of the political atmosphere?
00:47:13.114 --> 00:47:16.228 <v MORROW> In Taiwan?
00:47:16.228 --> 00:47:21.983 <v JOU> In Taiwan and also in the world.
00:47:21.983 --> 00:49:58.000 <v MORROW> I was living, first of all, in Taiwan. And the world then was much more compartmentalized probably than it is now. We didn't have internet. We didn't have anything like the immediate communication that links places around the planet instantaneously. Even getting to Taiwan and from the U.S.. Leaving from Seattle, where I flew, you would fly to Tokyo. You would spend the night—at least the way I did it—I ended up spending a night in Tokyo at the airport. The first place I landed in Asia was in Japan. I remember there were two really funny things about flying to—about going to Japan or arriving in Asia. I was really, very excited about going to Asia. And I think I flew on Northwest Orient Airline, the old Minneapolis-based airline that flew from Seattle to Tokyo. And I remember that they had hot towels on the plane. I'd never experienced a hot towel before. And then we arrived in Tokyo, and I looked out at the old—it's Haneda Airport, and I looked out the window as we were taxiing in, and here were two guys. They were obvious, they were workers on the runway of the airport, and they were playing catch with baseball mitts while they were waiting for planes. Something seemed very strange to me, but the Japanese, even then—back in the '60s—were fascinated with American baseball. And it was something you would not see at an American airport, where there was two workers who were not busy playing catch with a baseball. But anyway, I ended up spending a night in Tokyo before I went on to Taiwan.
00:49:58.000 --> 00:52:38.000 <v MORROW> And that distance gap permeated, continued to affect my whole experience in Taiwan. And it was further affected because Taiwan at that time was essentially a fascist place. Chiang Kai-shek was still very much in charge. The Cultural Revolution was happening in China. Something like an extreme anti-communist dampening on all political social economic activity in Taiwan existed. It was illegal to have a transistor radio without a headphone because they were afraid you were going to listen to broadcasts from the mainland. I got myself into trouble a couple of times while I was there speaking out against this Kuomintang fascistic curtailment of free speech or free activity. I almost got arrested once when I went to see Peng Ming-min. He was under house arrest. He was a Taiwan independence dissident. He ended up going into exile in Sweden, but at that time he was under house arrest. I managed to get through—they had his house surrounded by security police, but I snuck past them and got into his house and interviewed him and then got arrested after I came out. Not really arrested—I was detained, let's put it in these because I was an American student and they warned me and so on. Took my address and so on. I wasn't really arrested, but I was made to feel the force of the security service. Now, that was maybe the first time. Subsequently, I've had many, many encounters with security services and I learned not to be so intimidated by them. Anyway, that was my first experience of that type in Taiwan.
00:52:38.000 --> 00:55:02.885 <v MORROW> But coming back to your question, I mean, I was living in part because again, I was—it was part of my extension of my Dartmouth experience. I was seeing myself in Taiwan with it. I always felt that I had very limited time to absorb whatever opportunity I was given. And I took it all very seriously, probably as I said, too seriously. And so I was always engaged either in learning Chinese or doing something in the environment in which I was. And then I became, as I said, at the bars in downtown Taipei, the American GIs would hang out there and I would hang out with them and learn something about Vietnam. I was just this very intense young man. And so I was not paying a great deal of attention to what was going on back in the U.S. And I think from that period on, even after I went to Vietnam and so on, even though once I was in Vietnam, I was, of course, much closer to Americans. I became a journalist attached to the American military, but I was always living this somewhat isolated, somewhat alienated existence. And I think it's only in my later years—thanks to the internet really—that I've become much more involved and engaged, if you will, in American society, albeit remotely, because I've never lived back in North America, either in the U.S or Canada, for extended periods of time since that time.
00:55:02.885 --> 00:55:08.152 <v JOU> And how did your parents feel after they learned about you staying in Asia?
00:55:08.152 --> 01:03:56.460 <v MORROW> It was very interesting. You know, my mother—I told you my mother had a nervous breakdown when I was 13. And even in this period, my mother was still heavily medicated. My mother came back to live with us. My father took very good care of my mother for the rest of his life. She never went back to work. But up until this time, and for many years afterwards, my mother was a non-factor because she was present, but she was not present. She was, generally speaking, only half there because of the medicated situation in which she was living. But my father, who was, to be fair to him, was always very supportive of me, even though I argued with my father all the time, from the time I was very young. But my father never tried to suppress these arguments or impose his own views on me. He would treat me as an equal. And especially after I went off to Dartmouth—my father had left home when he was 16 and only actually got a high school diploma much later by correspondence when he was, I think, almost 30 years old. He had lived a very rough life as a migrant worker in the U.S. and Canada and all the way up to Alaska and had been a smuggler during prohibition, and this is also part of my interest in Chinese. I neglected to say because my father and my uncle had both smuggled Chinese into the U.S. They had a boat, a fast boat on the coast between—that ran across the Canadian border up from more or less Victoria down. They ran whiskey and they ran guns out to Sun Yat-sen and brought some illegal Chinese into this. And they had contacts with the triads in Seattle. I grew up with all these stories, which my mother didn't want my father to teach—tell my brother and I—but my father always shared this with us. And anyway, after I went off, he wasn't opposed to my making this decision. I ran out of money a few times in Vietnam, and he would send me money. And he eventually, before I got thrown out of Vietnam, he actually made a trip to Saigon and went down with me to talk with students at Saigon University, changed his own views. My father was a supporter of—he was a working class Democrat and so a supporter of [John F.] Kennedy, a supporter of [Lyndon B.] Johnson, supporter of Hubert Humphrey. But as my own views became more outspoken on the war and they were based on my reporting from the war, my father changed his stance and became not only a supporter of me, but a supporter of my views that the war was a mistake. And as I said, came to Vietnam, went with me to talk to students who were against the war, Vietnamese students at Saigon University. And he was by this time a man in his early seventies. I always had the support of my father. Ironically, to finish my mother's story, this whole experience started to bring my mother out of her malaise. And eventually, shortly after the war ended, my father died, relatively young. And my mother was also much, much younger than my father. When they had married, he was in his 40s and she was in her early 20s. She had been a nurse at the hospital and he'd gotten sick and they'd just fallen in love and she'd taken care of him. But it was a very unusual marriage, both because of their very different philosophical or worldviews, but also because of the age gap between them. And probably, as I said, this had also contributed to my mother's breaking down eventually under all the stress in our family, which was not intentional on my father's part. My father didn't drink; he didn't beat up my mother; didn't beat up me; didn't beat up anybody. But he had very strong views and he was always an intellectual without an education. He read a lot, but he had no formal education. And very opinionated and always willing to stand up to authority, very anti-authoritarian. My mother anyway, as my father grew weaker—as he got older and then died—all of a sudden my mother just came back to life. And my mother lived to be almost 100, and she regained her sanity, if you will. It was really interesting. After my father died, she developed an independent life for herself, and she became her own person again. And it's ironic, but she also became, even in that period, she became interested. I guess she became, in my mother's case, she just became worried about me because, yeah, I had a lot of adventures, if you will. I was almost killed several times, and I was a prisoner of war, all these things. My father accepted. Of course, he worried, but my father accepted that this was an existential path I had taken, he would support it. My mother, I think, just maybe it helped her in some ways to have some—to come out of her own meditative state or solipsistic state to become at least worried about me. And I think it may have played some role, although I think my father's death ultimately played a bigger role than my mother actually regaining her sanity and her own control over her own life.
01:03:56.460 --> 01:04:19.023 <v JOU> Great. Awesome. I think this is a good time to end our first session. And then for our next session, I wanted to continue on with our conversation on your time reporting in Vietnam and Dispatch News and all of that. How does that sound, Mike?
01:04:19.023 --> 01:09:24.359 <v MORROW> Yeah, that's fine. I'll just append one last thing about my early life I think that's important, and especially my relationship with my father. After my mother had become sick, and this before I went off to Dartmouth, but it was also very formative to me—formative for me. We had moved to this rural part of central or eastern Washington, as I said. I had spent this one summer as a pedicab driver. Even one year before, when I was only 16, at that time there were no Hispanic farm workers. In the summertime, kids from the area where I was, or some kids, walked about as migrant workers. And usually, again, they were a little bit older, but I was only 16 and I said "I want to do this." And my father accepted it and even encouraged me to do it because he had done something similar under more difficult circumstances when he was a boy. He had to leave because the family was poor. But I had spent a whole summer wandering up the Columbia and the Okanagan River all the way up the Canadian border, even jumping freight trains and living very rough and living with tough, mostly white working class, a lot of alcoholics, Some Native Americans also. Everybody working as a migrant worker in ranches, busting hay, or down in the valleys, in the orchards, spraying chemicals or thinning fruit or whatever. You just work for a few days at a farm and move on. Wherever they have work and move on. That had been the start of my father's really encouraging me to engage relatively high-risk situations. Looking back on it, I have six kids now. I would never, I have never—I still have one little one. I would never encourage any of them to do or even permit any of them to do what my father acquiesced, if not encouraged me to do, when I was 16. And it was dangerous too. I was with people who—I did have adventures there and encounters there that were—it could have turned out very badly. But just to finish with my father's influence on my life, he was always quite willing to accept a certain amount of, I think, concern. He could not, not have been concerned about my wellbeing, but he always encouraged me. He didn't tell me to do these things, but if I said I wanted to do them, he would support them, and he would support me to do them even though we were always arguing. It was only really after my father died that I fully appreciated him. I always thought I knew more than my father. I was very arrogant in terms of, especially after I went to Dartmouth, he considered myself to be an educated person. I had a certain disdain for my father that caused me to think I knew more than he did. But with hindsight, I realized that he was a very wise man.
01:09:24.359 --> 01:09:33.359 <v JOU> Alright, great. Thank you for sharing that, Mike. Okay, I'm gonna pause—well I'm gonna stop the recording here.
